environment.name: dungeon
environment.definition: Underground adventure locations such as crypts, tombs, labyrinths, and caverns.

environment.name: sea
environment.definition: Adventures on rivers, lakes, coasts, and open sea using vessels.

marching_order.rule: Establish party marching order when entering the dungeon.
Marching order depends largely on passage width.
Characters generally march in pairs, side by side, forming a line of pairs.
Marching order should be written down so position is always clear.
If using a large map, dice, tokens, or miniatures may represent positions.

mapping.rule: One player should be designated as mapper.
The mapper records explored areas so the group does not get lost and knows what has been explored.
Dungeons are typically mapped on graph paper with 1/4 inch square grids at a scale of 10 feet per square.
If the mapper's character dies, mapping duties pass to a player with a living character; in-game, the surviving character takes the dead character's map.

movement.rate: Full dungeon exploration movement rate, normally 120 feet per turn unless heavily encumbered.

uses.use: Searching a 10' x 10' area for secret doors or traps.

movement.rate: One-third of exploration movement per round, normally 40 feet per round unless heavily encumbered.
Full character speed per round, normally 120 feet unless heavily encumbered.

map_scale.rule: On large play maps, one square commonly equals 5 feet.
All distances may be measured precisely on the map grid.

authority.rule: The Judge is the final authority on what may be accomplished in a given period of time.

rest.rule: Characters may remain active for 5 turns before needing 1 turn of rest.

penalty_for_skipping_rest.rule: If characters continue without resting, all suffer -1 to attack throws and damage rolls.
penalty_for_skipping_rest.duration: Until they have rested for 1 turn.

light_effects.rule: Characters or monsters carrying a light source cannot surprise opponents.

infravision.definition: Ability to see in darkness to a limited distance, usually 60 feet.

limitations.rule: Does not allow reading or seeing fine detail.
Any visible light, normal or magical, disrupts infravision.

attack_penalty_for_no_sight.rule: Creatures unable to see due to darkness, blindness, or invisibility of target suffer -4 on attacks.

standard_door.definition: Heavy wooden door reinforced with iron banding.

pick_lock.rule: A thief may pick a lock in 1 turn with a successful open locks proficiency throw.

batter_down.rule: Any character with an axe can batter down a standard dungeon door in 3 turns.
batter_down.sturdy_metal_or_stone_door: Cannot generally be battered down without heavy equipment.

modifiers.rule: Unusual size or material may impose a penalty.
For each point of Strength adjustment, modify the die roll by +/-4.
If two characters cooperate, use the stronger character's Strength adjustment and add +4.

stuck_doors.retry: Characters may try again if they fail.

evil_doors.rule: Evil doors automatically swing shut when released unless spiked or wedged open.
Evil doors always open easily for monsters unless spiked shut, held firm, or magically closed.

secret_doors.definition: Concealed or hidden doors such as sliding panels or trapdoors.

search_requirements.rule: Characters must specifically declare they are looking for secret doors.
Searching a 10' x 10' area takes 1 turn.
Each character gets only one chance to find each secret door.

listening_at_doors_or_intersections.thief_note: Thieves use their own hear noise chance from thief skills.
listening_at_doors_or_intersections.attempt_limit: One attempt per character per door or intersection.
listening_at_doors_or_intersections.exception: Some creatures, such as undead, do not make noise.

searching_for_traps.scope: All classes can search for non-magical traps.

requirements.rule: They must search the correct location.
Searching takes 1 turn per 10' x 10' area.
One roll per character per location.

trap_triggering.rule: Traps have specific triggers such as opening a door or stepping on a specific area.
trap_triggering.trigger_check: Whenever an action could trigger a trap, the Judge rolls 1d6.

trap_effects.general_rule: Each trap has a specific effect depending on type.

other_traps.rule: Some traps allow a saving throw to reduce or avoid effects.
Some traps only deal damage on a successful attack throw.

marching_and_mapping.rule: Wilderness marching and mapping function like other adventures.
The party travels in an established marching order.
The mapper records progress in unexplored areas, unless the party already has a map.
The Judge uses a prepared map.

mapping_scales.scale: Standard wilderness map: 6 miles per hex.
Larger area map: 24 miles per hex.

distance_scale.rule: Distances are measured in yards rather than feet.
distance_scale.conversion: A character who moves 120 feet per turn in a dungeon moves 120 yards per turn in the wilderness.
distance_scale.rule: Weapon and spell ranges are measured in yards in the wilderness.

party_rate.rule: A traveling party moves at the rate of its slowest member.

terrain_multipliers.rule: The listed miles per day assume an 8-hour day through open, clear terrain before modifiers.
Other terrain features such as canyons or large rivers may further slow travel at the Judge's discretion.

forced_march.benefit: Increase miles traveled that day by 50%.
forced_march.cost: Characters must rest for 24 hours afterward.

routine_rest.rule: During normal wilderness travel, characters must rest one day per six days of travel.

penalty_for_insufficient_rest.rule: Characters who do not get proper rest suffer a cumulative -1 penalty on attack throws and damage rolls per day.

time_scale.rule: While traveling in the wilderness, time is usually tracked in days unless an encounter occurs.
Turns are not commonly used in wilderness adventures.

safe_travel.rule: Following trails, roads, and clear landmarks prevents becoming lost.

lost_check.timing: At the start of each day of overland travel.
lost_check.procedure: The Judge makes a proficiency throw against the terrain's navigation target.
lost_check.navigation_bonus: If any party member has Navigation proficiency, the party gains +4 on the throw.

when_lost.rule: If the party becomes lost, the Judge decides their actual direction of travel and how far off course they are.

daily_consumption.rule: Each character must consume 1 stone of food and drink per day.

lack_of_food.rule: No significant effect for the first two days without sufficient food.

recovery.rule: Eating enough food for one day restores natural healing.
Lost hit points then recover at the normal rate.

after_one_day.continued_damage: Lose an additional 1d4 hit points per day thereafter.
after_one_day.healing_loss: Healing ability is lost when the first die of damage is rolled.

foraging.check: Proficiency throw 18+ on 1d20 per day of travel.

hunting.activity: Must be the only activity for the day; no travel is possible.
hunting.additional_rule: One wandering monster check is made during the day of hunting using the appropriate terrain table.

survival_proficiency_bonus.rule: Characters with Survival proficiency gain +4 on hunt and forage throws.

movement.rule: Long-distance air movement equals normal land miles per day multiplied by 2.
movement.example_equivalent: 120' normal movement corresponds to 48 miles per day by air.

carrying_capacity_by_hd.rule: Winged beasts may carry riders or burdens in size increments based on Hit Dice multiples of 3.

capacity_examples_as_rules.entry: May carry a dwarf or human child.
May carry an adult human or elf, or two dwarves.
May carry large animals such as horses, or four adult humans.
May carry a very large animal, or four horses, or eight humans.

general_rules.rule: Characters do not map or march at sea; they sail or row on vessels.
Some vessels can be handled by an adventuring party; others require many sailors or rowers.
Structural hit points function like normal hit points for creatures.
If a vessel is reduced to 0 or fewer structural hit points, it can no longer move and ship weapons no longer function.
A ship sinks 1d10 rounds after being reduced to 0 structural hit points.
Long-distance sea movement depends on vessel type and weather.
Miles per day on the Sea Vessels table assume a 12-hour day of travel.
Ships under sail may travel 24 hours per day if a qualified navigator is aboard, potentially doubling distance per day.
This 24-hour sailing multiplier is in addition to weather modifiers.
The 24-hour multiplier does not apply if the ship stops each night, if it is under oar, if it is traveling along a coastline, or if it lacks the minimum number of regular crewmen.
Sailing against the wind requires tacking and reduces movement rates by two rows on the wind conditions table.

row.cell: Prevailing wind direction for this locale

becalmed.rule: Oared ships may still move at rowing rate.

very_strong_winds.rule: Sailing against the wind is not possible.

gale.rule: Sailing against the wind is not possible.
Ships exposed to a gale may be damaged or sunk.

rowed_vessels.rule: Galleys and other rowed vessels must make a saving throw of 16+ each hour or be sunk.
Even on a successful saving throw, the vessel takes double gale damage.

coastal_escape.rule: Galleys in sight of a coastline may beach to avoid the gale.
If the coast is clear terrain, they beach automatically.
Otherwise they need a navigation throw of 14+ to find a safe beach or cove.

lost_check.timing: At the start of each day of sea travel.
lost_check.procedure: The Judge makes a proficiency throw against the listed navigation value.
lost_check.navigation_bonus: If any party member has Navigation proficiency, the party gets +4.

when_lost.rule: If the party becomes lost, the Judge decides its actual direction and how far it is off the intended course.
The Judge should describe wind direction according to the direction the group believes it is traveling until they discover the error.

food_and_water.rule: Sea voyages use wilderness food and water rules.

rowers.water_requirement: 3 gallons of water per day rather than 1 gallon.
rowers.encumbrance: 3 stone per day of water supplies.

rations.rule: Standard rations are perishable and become inedible after one week.
Long sea voyages therefore commonly rely on iron rations.

scurvy.trigger: One month at sea eating iron rations without fresh fruit, onions, or potatoes.
scurvy.effect: Lose 1 point of STR and 1 point of CON each week.
scurvy.death: If either ability reaches 0, the character dies.
scurvy.recovery: Eating fresh food restores 3 points each of STR and CON per week.

fishing.requirement: Ship must be becalmed or anchored.
fishing.check: Each fishing character may attempt a proficiency throw of 14+ on 1d20 each day.
fishing.survival_bonus: +4 if the character has Survival proficiency.

general_rule.rule: Only characters who survive an adventure receive XP.

civilization_requirement.rule: Treasure XP is awarded only for treasure recovered from the dungeon or wilderness and brought back to civilization.

award_rate.rule: Characters gain 1 XP per 1 gp value of coin, gems, jewelry, and special treasure recovered on adventures.

equipment_recovered.rule: Recovered equipment must be sold immediately for coin to grant XP.
If kept for later use, it grants no XP.

magic_items.rule: If a recovered magic item is sold without being used, it grants 1 XP per 1 gp earned in sale.
If the item is used, it grants no XP, even if later sold.

non_qualifying_sources.rule: Wages and business transactions do not grant treasure XP.
Recovering monster parts does not grant treasure XP; that counts under monster experience.

qualifying_defeats.rule: Defeated monsters grant XP whether outsmarted, captured, or killed.

calculation.rule: Each monster has a base XP by Hit Dice and a bonus XP per special ability.
Count special abilities by the number of asterisks next to the monster's Hit Dice in its listing.
calculation.formula: Total monster XP = base XP + (bonus XP per ability x number of special abilities).

notes.note: For monsters of HD 22 and higher, add a cumulative 250 XP to both Base and Bonus categories for each additional HD step.

allocating_xp.rule: Total treasure XP and monster XP are added together.
The total is divided evenly among all surviving party members and henchmen.

eligibility.rule: Only characters alive when the party returns to civilization receive XP.
Characters slain during the adventure but raised before returning to civilization do receive XP.

adjustments_to_xp.rule: Prime requisite XP bonuses or penalties are applied to the individual character's final XP award.

procedure.step: Record the new level, title, and XP needed for the next level.
Roll additional hit points using the appropriate hit die and Constitution modifier; gain at least 1 hp regardless of Constitution.
Record any new or improved class abilities.
Choose any new proficiencies and spells for which the character is eligible.
Update attack throws and saving throws.

restriction.rule: A character can never gain enough XP from one adventure to advance two or more levels.

heirs_and_inheritance.rule: With the Judge's permission, a new character may be the heir of the dead character.
The Judge may allow a will leaving treasure to an heir.

banking_requirement.rule: If treasure is left formally through a bank, it must be stored with a reputable bank.
banking_requirement.cost: The bank charges 10% of the treasure.

default_heir_level.rule: Unless the player begins as an existing henchman, an heir starts as a new 1st level character.
A player may leave a character inheritance only one time.

reserve_xp_fund.definition: A reserve fund of experience points that an heir may use if the original character is permanently killed.
reserve_xp_fund.value: 90% of the gold piece value of money allocated to the reserve.

allocation_requirement.rule: Money must be spent for no tangible in-game benefit whatsoever.

zero_level_characters_and_adventuring_xp.rule: A 0th level character can earn adventuring XP.
zero_level_characters_and_adventuring_xp.advancement_threshold: At 100 XP, the character becomes a 1st level fighter.

on_becoming_fighter.rule: Gain fighter class proficiency, powers, attack throws, and saving throws.
Re-roll hit points using 1d8, keeping either the new total or the old total, whichever is higher.

erosion_of_general_proficiencies.rule: At 2nd, 3rd, and 4th level, remove one of the pre-existing general proficiencies each time.

adventuring_proficiency_gain.rule: At 4th level, the character gains Adventuring proficiency.

class_restriction.rule: Under normal circumstances, 0th level characters advancing from adventuring XP become fighters, not other classes.

general_definition.encounter: Any meeting between adventurers and potential enemies during adventures.

time_scale.rule: Any encounter lasting 60 rounds or less counts as one full turn for adventure timekeeping.

encounter_sequence.step: Encounter begins when the Judge places or rolls an encounter.
Judge determines encounter distance, usually 2d6 x 10 feet unless already known.
Judge determines surprise for the characters and/or monsters.
Judge decides monster action; players decide character action such as fight, flee, or talk.
If either side fights, combat begins and time proceeds in rounds.
Unsurprised characters roll initiative and act in initiative order.
Initiative is rolled again at the start of each round.
Encounter usually ends when one side dies or flees.

encounter_distance_limitations.rule: Dungeon layout and available light sources may limit encounter distance.

general_rules.rule: Wilderness encounters follow the same general sequence as dungeon encounters.

visibility_rules.rule: Man-sized targets are visible from up to 1,000 yards over flat plains.
Larger creatures can see and be seen at proportionally greater distances.
Elevation such as towers or hills also increases spotting distance proportionally relative to a 6-foot person.

general_rules.rule: Sea encounters are similar to wilderness encounters.
A ship can never surprise a monster native to the water.

distances.monster_distance: Use plains encounter distance: 5d20 x 10 yards, modified by monster size.
distances.other_ship_visibility: Up to 6 miles in normal weather.
distances.land_visibility: Up to 24 miles in normal weather.

visibility_reduction.rule: Harsh weather or dense fog may reduce normal visibility distances by 90%.
The Judge may instead apply another penalty depending on conditions.

number_encountered.definition: Monster entries list a Number Encountered range for one meeting.
number_encountered.rule: The actual number encountered depends on whether monsters are wandering or in lair, and whether the encounter is in wilderness or dungeon.
In dungeons, the number encountered also varies by dungeon level.

when_used.rule: Used when characters and monsters encounter each other unexpectedly.
The Judge may roll for one side, both sides, or only the side that could reasonably be surprised.

surprised.rule: Surprised opponents are caught off guard for one round.
Attacks against them gain +2 to the attack throw.
They do not receive shield benefit, if any.

both_sides_surprised.rule: If all participants on both sides are surprised, no one acts in the first round.
Second round initiative is rolled normally.

ready.rule: Ready creatures may act in the first round.

modifiers.rule: Well-hidden or naturally stealthy creatures may impose a penalty on the other side's surprise roll.
Some creatures or classes are less likely to be surprised and may gain a bonus on the roll.

general_rule.rule: Sneaking is resolved using surprise rolls and hearing noises throws, depending on how alert the observers are.

observer_state.rule: Characters attempting to sneak through are detected automatically.
observer_state.duration_limit: Most monsters cannot maintain this level of alertness for more than one turn.
observer_state.exceptions: Constructs and undead are always actively alert.

procedure.step: Judge makes a surprise roll for the monsters when characters attempt to sneak.
If monsters are surprised, characters move for one round undetected.
If monsters are ready, the sneaking characters are detected.
Judge makes hearing noises throws for the monsters, normally 18+ on 1d20.
If all fail, characters move for one round undetected.
If at least one succeeds, that monster hears something.
Judge then makes a surprise roll to determine whether the sneaking characters are actually detected.

probabilities_from_text.passive_monster: Under normal circumstances, a passive monster can be snuck up on 33% of the time.
probabilities_from_text.distracted_monster: Under normal circumstances, a distracted monster can be snuck up on 90% of the time.

alertness_proficiency_effect.rule: A monster with Alertness is surprised only on 1 in 6.
A monster with Alertness gains +4 to Hear Noise.

resulting_probabilities.passive_monster_with_alertness: Chance of sneaking up drops to 16%.
resulting_probabilities.distracted_monster_with_alertness: Chance of sneaking up drops to 75%.

thief_interaction.rule: If a dimly lit area or concealment exists, a thief or similar class may attempt to hide in shadows.
If successful, monsters do not see the thief and are treated as distracted for detection purposes.
The thief is then detected only if the monsters hear him make noise.
If the thief also successfully moves silently, he cannot be heard.

monsters_sneaking.rule: Monsters may sneak using the same mechanics.
Characters then rely on surprise rolls and/or hear noise throws to detect them.

when_used.rule: Use a reaction roll when monster response to the party is not obvious.

procedure.step: Apply the lead character's Charisma bonus or penalty.

reaction_results.unfriendly: Dislike the adventurers and will attack if it is reasonable to do so.
reaction_results.neutral: Will consider letting adventurers live if they parley; not necessarily friendly.
reaction_results.indifferent: Will ignore adventurers if possible and negotiate if necessary.
reaction_results.friendly: Likes the adventurers and may cooperate in mutually beneficial ways.

friendly_monsters.rule: Friendly monsters may be recruited as hirelings with a successful roll on the Reaction to Hiring Offer table.

judge_interpretation.rule: The Judge must interpret results in context.
The Judge may alter the rolled reaction if another result is more plausible in the circumstances.

general_rule.rule: When one side flees and the other chases, a chase begins.
Characters choose when to flee and whether to pursue fleeing monsters.
Whether monsters pursue fleeing characters is determined by a Monster Reaction roll; a result of 2-8 means they pursue.

automatic_escape_before_combat.rule: If combat has not commenced and the fleeing side has higher movement, it can always escape.

chase_start.rule: Otherwise the chase begins when the fleeing side starts moving on its initiative number.

movement_hazards.rule: During pursuit, when a character passes through a doorway, makes a hard turn, or similar maneuver, the Judge may require a saving throw versus Paralysis with Dexterity bonus added.

failure_effect.rule: On failure, the character falls, moves no further that round, and may stand and make a full move on next round's initiative.

catching_up.rule: If pursuers are within 5 feet at the start of a round, they may begin melee combat.
If the fleeing side continues fleeing after pursuers reach melee range, use Defensive Movement rules.

ending_pursuit.adventurers: Players decide when adventurers stop pursuing monsters.

monsters.rule: A monster stops chasing if adventurers get out of its line of sight.
If monsters value treasure, there is a 50% chance they stop to collect treasure the party drops (4-6 on 1d6).
Hungry or less intelligent monsters may similarly stop for dropped food.

automatic_escape_on_surprise.rule: If one side is surprised in a wilderness encounter, the other side can automatically flee successfully.

evasion_check.rule: Otherwise, the fleeing party must succeed on the Wilderness Evasion table.
The larger the pursuing group relative to the fleeing group, the easier it is for the fleeing side to escape.

columns.column: Modifier if Pursuers are Up to 25% of Evading Group

judge_modifiers.rule: The Judge may modify the probabilities for conditions and environment.

examples_converted_to_rules.rule: Densely wooded terrain may give a bonus to flee.
A much faster pursuing party may gain a bonus to catch the fleeing side.

if_evasion_fails.rule: The pursuers keep the fleeing party within sight.
If the pursuers have greater movement, they have a 50% chance (11+ on d20) to catch up close.
If that catch-up roll fails, the fleeing side may attempt to escape again.
This cycle repeats daily until either the fleeing side escapes or the pursuers catch them.

general_rule.rule: When sea vessels or sea monsters meet, one side may try to flee.
Initial distance is determined as a normal encounter.
Escape depends primarily on speed difference.

successful_evasion.rule: If evasion succeeds, pursuers cannot try again for 24 hours, and then only if a random encounter roll produces an encounter.

failed_evasion.rule: If evasion fails, the pursuer begins at the spotted distance and starts gaining.

gain_rate.rule: If the pursuer is slower than the fleeing party, or no more than 30 feet per round faster, it gains at 30 feet (10 yards) per round.
If the pursuer is more than 30 feet per round faster, it gains by the full speed difference each round.
